title: Shankara in the king's body
hook: Shankara leaves his body in a cave and lives as a king, and behind the story sits an old teaching: you are not your body, or even your mind
carry: you wear the body; you are the seer

segments.voice: Yesterday: fourteen years to walk on water. The powers are obstacles, not the goal.
screen: `THE BOATMAN'S PENNY — POWERS AREN'T THE GOAL.`

segments.voice: Tradition tells a story about the great teacher Shankara. He has just won a famous debate against the scholar Mandana Mishra, and Mandana's wife, the brilliant Ubhaya Bharati, takes up the challenge herself. She asks him about love between husband and wife. Shankara, a lifelong monk, has no answer. So he asks for time. He leaves his own body in a cave, guarded by his students, and enters the body of a king who has just died. He lives as that king for a while, learns what he needs, and comes back. Today's sutras name that very power, and others just as startling.
screen: `A DEBATE ABOUT LOVE.` → `A MONK WITH NO ANSWER.` → `HE ENTERS A KING'S BODY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.38: by loosening what binds the mind to one body, and knowing the mind's pathways, the mind can enter another body. Para-sharira-avesha. More follow. 3.39: master udana, the upward breath, and the body rises. 3.40: master samana, the breath at the center, and a radiance. The classical commentators read these as real. They can, because of what Hindu thought says a person is. In the Samkhya-Yoga picture, the body is made of nature, prakriti. So is the mind, just far subtler. That's how a mind might move from one body to another, the way Shankara did. But neither one is you. You are the seer, purusha, the one who watches body and mind. The Upanishads call it atman, the self. And the Gita gives the picture every Hindu child hears: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves worn-out bodies and takes on new. That's what Hindus mean by rebirth. It's also why, at a Hindu funeral, many families say the one who wore the body has gone on. Shankara, in the story, didn't stay a king. He learned what he came for, and went back to his own body and his work. Today that's worth remembering on the days the body feels like everything: a mirror, an illness, an age. You wear it, and it matters. It isn't the whole of you.
screen: `PARA-SHARIRA-AVESHA: ANOTHER BODY.` · `BODY AND MIND: BOTH PRAKRITI.` · `THE SEER: PURUSHA, ATMAN.` · `THE GITA: WORN-OUT CLOTHES.` · then, large: `YOU WEAR THE BODY; YOU ARE THE SEER.`

segments.voice: Sit and feel the body: its weight on the seat, the breath moving in and out. Then notice that something is noticing all this. Thoughts come too, and that same something notices them. Don't try to pin it down. Just rest as the one who watches, a little lighter than the body being watched.
Para-sharira-avesha, entering another's body. The first of today's powers, with levitation and radiance, which the classical commentators read as real attainments of mastery.
Your line: you wear the body; you are the seer. Shankara stepped out, and came home. That's day four seventy-four.

howItsDone: Hindus widely teach that the self (atman) is not the body, a teaching voiced in the Bhagavad Gita and behind belief in rebirth; the classical commentaries on the Yoga Sutras treat these powers as real within the Samkhya-Yoga view, and the traditional life of Shankara tells of one used briefly and set aside.

prakriti.meaning: nature, the stuff of both mind and body

purusha.meaning: the seer, pure awareness, in Samkhya-Yoga

atman.meaning: the self, which the Upanishads say is not the body
